analysis.title: Impact Series 15: The global energy race
key_insights: Barclays frames the energy transition as an expansion of the whole energy system, not a substitution. Demand for electricity, oil, gas and renewables is rising at once, driven by electrification, AI, digital infrastructure, demographics and development.
Barclays' proprietary global energy model forecasts energy demand growth of 1.9% per year over 2025-2050, above the EIA's current forecast.

Capex across the energy sector (oil and gas, LNG, power, grids, renewables, electrification) is estimated to reach $3.6trn annually by 2027, more than three times the capital currently required for planned AI infrastructure development.
Barclays says the most acute capital shortfalls are in transmission networks, storage and grid infrastructure. Grid investment was about $400bn in 2024 against about $1trn in generation assets.

In 2025 oil, natural gas, coal, solar, wind and nuclear all set record use. Clean energy investment reached a record $2.3trn in 2025, more than double the roughly $1trn into fossil fuels, yet global demand growth of 1.3% still needed more oil, gas and coal.

Global upstream capital expenditure is still roughly 45% below peak. Barclays expects underlying oil demand growth above 6 million barrels per day over 2025-2030, while the industry must replace more than 7 million barrels per day of output annually just to hold supply.

Barclays forecasts global oil demand growth of about 1.1mb/d a year over 2027-2030, reaching 110.6mb/d by 2030. It says current prices underestimate this tightness, leaving commodity prices vulnerable to upside pressure.

Data centre electricity use is forecast at 565 TWh in 2026, up 26% from 447 TWh in 2025. Related power demand is 132 GW this year and could reach 290 GW by 2030. AI-optimised servers are 31% of data centre power use, up from about 20% a year ago.

By 2040 Barclays estimates more than 600GW of data centre capacity will need about 32 quad Btu of energy, roughly equal to Russia's 2025 energy use and slightly below India's. Data centres would be about 12% of the increase in global energy use by 2040.

US installed data centre IT capacity is expected to rise from 34GW in 2025 to over 110GW by 2029. Global capacity additions are about 25GW in 2026 and more than 30GW in 2027. Hyperscalers are expected to take about 60% of additions (ex-China), and many non-hyperscaler projects may not be built.
EVs are expected to reach nearly 60% of the global vehicle fleet by 2050. Transport's share of global energy use falls to about 14% from 17.5%.

Refining is tight: permanent closures and war damage cut global refinery output by an estimated 4.5 million barrels per day in Q2 2026. The US 3-2-1 crack spread hit $64 per barrel and global refining margins touched $59.

Grid investment needs to rise about 50% by 2030, from roughly $400bn to over $600bn a year, per the IEA. More than 2,500GW of renewable, storage and large-load projects are stalled in grid connection queues.

Barclays is particularly constructive on nuclear, citing decarbonisation, energy security and AI power demand, and says the sector is experiencing a renaissance. It says being positive on clean energy deployment is not the same as being bullish on clean-tech manufacturers, because Chinese scale compresses margins. Value may accrue to developers with contracted demand and to scarcer enabling assets such as transmission, transformers, storage and grid software.

Barclays argues energy demand could keep inflation higher for longer through higher baseline inflation, greater inflation volatility and more frequent shocks, with risks skewed to the upside. It says AI-related electricity costs are a measurable contributor to the rise in core PCE.

US permitting is a bottleneck: developers may face more than 60 permits and reviews, nearly one-third of completed milestones across 104 federal-system projects were late, almost 30% of large energy projects were cancelled or paused, and only 39% of environmental impact statements met the 2-year deadline set by the 2023 Fiscal Responsibility Act.

Physical AI (humanoids, autonomous vehicles, industrial automation, drones) could become a $1trn ecosystem by 2035 and add a new class of electricity demand. A humanoid such as Tesla Optimus uses roughly 500 watts walking, and humans are 40-45% more energy efficient for the same activity.

sector_views.rationale: Barclays is particularly constructive on nuclear given its role in decarbonisation, energy security and AI-related power demand.
Barclays identifies transmission, transformers, storage and grid software as the scarcest enabling assets and the most acute shortfall in the energy system.
Chinese manufacturing scale has compressed margins across commoditised parts of the value chain, so clean energy deployment is not the same as bullish on manufacturers.

sector_views.sector: Oil and gas upstream and refining
sector_views.rationale: Upstream capex is about 45% below peak against rising demand, and refining capacity shortfalls have pushed crack spreads to records.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Above the EIA's current forecast, supporting a multi-decade capital cycle.
Low-emissions sources supplied nearly 60% of growth, and the remaining 40% still required more oil, gas and coal.
More than twice the rate of total energy demand growth.
Barclays sees demand growth of about 1.1mb/d a year over 2027-2030, tighter than current prices imply.
Record level reflecting a structural shortage of refining capacity.
IEA estimate, with almost two-thirds directed to clean energy technologies and infrastructure.
Barclays estimate, reflecting the gap between supply capacity and required capacity.

macro_indicators.reading: AI-related electricity costs are a measurable contributor to the rise
macro_indicators.interpretation: Energy costs from AI demand are showing up in inflation data.

risk_factors: Supply fails to keep pace with demand because of permitting delays, infrastructure bottlenecks and underinvestment, leaving energy markets tighter for longer.
Grid connection constraints (more than 2,500GW stalled) could slow both the energy transition and the AI buildout.
Energy-driven inflation could be more persistent and more volatile than investors expect, with upside skew.
Non-hyperscaler data centre projects face execution bottlenecks and may not be built.
Geopolitical shocks (Iran, Ukraine) can disrupt energy flows and prices more severely in a tight market.
Clean-tech manufacturing margins are compressed by Chinese overcapacity.
charts_described: Figure 1 lists Barclays' forecasts for demand and supply to 2050, with global energy demand at 657.60 Quad Btu in 2025 rising to 885.61 by 2050 (1.2% CAGR) and AI/data centre demand rising from 0.21 to 11.18 Quad Btu.
Figure 5 shows global investment in energy 2016-2026e, split into fossil fuels and clean energy, approximated from the IEA.
Figure 8 compares global grid investment (about $400bn) with generation asset investment (about $1trn) in 2024.
vol_and_positioning: Barclays shows a Crude Oil ETF Volatility Index chart (Figure 16) but the text gives no levels.
Investors are positioning for a rise in the inflation risk premium, per Barclays.
geopolitical: US-Iran conflict in 2026 generated a large energy-price shock and threatened critical LNG transit routes.
Russia's invasion of Ukraine and Europe's forced pivot from Russian pipeline gas to LNG from the US, Qatar and others.
War-related damage and permanent closures cut global refinery output by an estimated 4.5 million barrels per day in Q2 2026.
Geopolitical fragmentation is pushing governments toward resilience-optimised energy supply, strategic reserves and long-term LNG contracts.
The Trump administration has used executive action to speed permitting for energy and data-centre projects, but Barclays says legislative reform is needed.
